notes: Murder-trial acquitees challenge lifting of DCI Caldwell's suspension; Wilkie J granted declaration that termination was unlawful.

enrichment.short_title: Coghlan v GMP: judicial review of lifting DCI Caldwell's suspension
key_facts: Five men acquitted after Penry-Davey J stayed their murder trial for abuse of process criticised DCI Caldwell's handling of disclosure, including missing NCS informant material on log 89.
DCI Caldwell was suspended on 15 September 2003 but the Chief Constable terminated the suspension on 20 October 2003, allowing him to return to duty before disciplinary proceedings concluded.
The claimants, discharged defendants in the Barnshaw murder investigation, sought a declaration that lifting suspension was unlawful.
DCC Green's decision failed to weigh the public interest in maintaining disciplinary proceedings after the trial judge's findings on Caldwell's conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a chief constable's decision to terminate a police officer's suspension pending discipline.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declaration granted that the decision of 20 October 2003 to lift DCI Caldwell's suspension was unlawful; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A chief constable deciding whether to lift suspension or permit retirement must have regard to the public interest in seeing disciplinary proceedings through; failure to consider that relevant factor renders the decision Wednesbury unreasonable even where non-statutory guidance is involved.
legal_issues: Whether lifting suspension ignored the public interest in completing police discipline after abuse-of-process findings
Legal effect of Secretary of State non-statutory guidance on suspension and retirement
Whether claimants had sufficient interest to challenge a decision about a third-party officer
Wednesbury review of DCC Green's balancing exercise

R (Khatun) v Newham LBC [2004] EWCA Civ 55

notes: Zimbabwean gay asylum appeal after remittal; Court of Appeal dismissed, distinguishing Australian S395 on covert homosexual conduct.

enrichment.short_title: Z v SSHD: Zimbabwe homosexuality asylum and S395 distinction

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Mr Z, a Zimbabwean homosexual, claimed asylum fearing persecution including from his ZANU-connected stepfather after declaring he wished to live with his partner Mr D.
The adjudicator disbelieved the stepfather account; the IAT on remittal held covert conduct meant no real risk of serious harm and article 8 was not engaged.
On appeal Mr Z relied on the High Court of Australia decision in Appellant S395/2002 on imputed identity and persecution of discreet homosexuals.
No sufficient evidence showed a settled intention to live openly with Mr D or that living together would attract persecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Immigration Appeal Tribunal remittal decision refusing asylum and human rights protection.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Covert homosexual conduct without evidence of intent to live together openly does not establish Refugee Convention persecution; the Australian S395 approach does not assist where factual issues were available for evidence at first instance but inadequately proved, and asylum could not protect rights to live with a partner remaining in Zimbabwe.
legal_issues: Application of Appellant S395/2002 to discreet homosexual asylum claims
Whether article 3 or 8 ECHR assists where Convention claim fails on facts
Adequacy of evidence on intent to live with a same-sex partner
Distinction between persecution for orientation and individualised hostility
linked_authorities: Appellant S395/2002 v Minister for Immigration [2003] HCA 71
SSHD v Ahmed [2002] Imm AR 560
R (Razgar) v SSHD [2004] 2 AC 368

notes: CCRC-referred manslaughter sentence appeal after drunken aggressive driving killed teenager; 11-year YOI sentence upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Ballard: gross negligence manslaughter sentence after drunken driving spree
key_facts: The 18-year-old appellant, heavily intoxicated after ejection from a nightclub, collected his car and drove repeated dangerous circuits outside the club.
He mounted pavements, performed handbrake turns and drove at groups before striking and killing a 17-year-old on a central reservation; breath tests showed about three times the legal limit.
The jury acquitted murder and unlawful-act manslaughter but convicted gross negligence manslaughter; Aikens J sentenced 11 years' detention in a YOI.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the sentence appeal, which the court considered manifestly excessive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal reference from the Criminal Cases Review Commission against an 11-year sentence for gross negligence manslaughter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the 11-year sentence was severe but not manifestly excessive; the CCRC reference was criticised as misjudged.
enrichment.ratio: Prolonged outrageously dangerous drunken driving putting many people at grave risk, even without specific intent towards the victim, can justify a manslaughter sentence well above authorities on single-incident dangerous driving because the case is not a conventional tariff comparison.
legal_issues: Whether 11 years was manifestly excessive for gross negligence manslaughter
Appropriate sentencing where jury excluded specific intent and unlawful act
Whether CCRC reference met section 13 real-possibility test
Comparison with causing death by dangerous driving authorities
linked_authorities: R v Ripley [1997] 1 Cr App R (S) 19
R v Wright [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 4
R v Galt (1995) 16 Cr App R (S) 1013

notes: Confiscation appeal on £1.1m cigarette duty evasion where defendant's reward was only £5,000; benefit held to be full pecuniary advantage.

enrichment.short_title: R v Ellingham: confiscation benefit for minor role in cigarette smuggling
key_facts: Ellingham pleaded guilty to fraudulent evasion of duty on about six million smuggled cigarettes with duty of £1,120,850 evaded via his company Vetaria Import & Export.
On his basis of plea he was a freight organiser paid £5,000, not the financier or end user of the smuggling operation.
A confiscation order of £129,756 was made representing his realisable assets after the full pecuniary advantage was conceded at £1,120,850.
He appealed arguing his benefit was limited to the £5,000 actually received.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against confiscation order following guilty plea to cigarette duty evasion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to the House of Lords and certification of a point of law of general public importance refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 71(4)-(5) a participant who obtains a pecuniary advantage by evading duty is treated as obtaining property equal to the full advantage avoided, even where his personal reward was much smaller and he lacked beneficial interest in the wider proceeds.
legal_issues: Whether benefit under section 71(4) is restricted to sums actually received
Application of section 71(5) pecuniary advantage to duty evasion
Human Rights Act compatibility of full-advantage confiscation
Distinction from Drugs Trafficking Act confiscation provisions
linked_authorities: R v Rezvi [2002] UKHL 1
R v Gibbons [2004] EWCA Crim 576
R v Smith [2001] 1 AC 146

notes: Habeas corpus challenge to Swedish extradition after nine-year delay; Collins J held return not oppressive.

enrichment.short_title: Kila v Brixton: habeas corpus and delayed Swedish extradition
key_facts: Parfait Kila, a Swedish national of Angolan origin, was convicted in Sweden of gross fraud in the mid-1990s and sentenced to two years but fled before starting his sentence.
Swedish authorities located him in London in 2002 and sought extradition; a warrant was executed in July 2004 after procedural delays.
Kila argued Swedish indifference and delay made return oppressive, especially as a ten-year Swedish limitation on enforcement approached in April 2005.
He had lived in the UK since about 1997, had a child abroad and was engaged to a British citizen.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court habeas corpus application challenging extradition to serve an outstanding Swedish fraud sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; extradition was not oppressive despite delay, though the court noted Swedish enforcement might expire after 13 April 2005.
enrichment.ratio: Mere delay in locating and extraditing a fugitive does not make return oppressive without more; approaching expiry of a foreign limitation period is not a reason to refuse extradition but underscores need to avoid further procedural delay.
legal_issues: Whether Swedish authorities' delay made extradition oppressive
Effect of approaching ten-year Swedish sentence limitation
Standard for habeas corpus where conviction is established abroad
Criticism of length of UK extradition processing

confidence.notes: Fact-heavy extradition judgment with clear dismissal though some evidential gaps noted.

notes: Beth Din freezing order and registered caution could not bind innocent purchasers after fraudulent house sale; proprietary estoppel claim failed.

enrichment.short_title: Kastner v Jason: Beth Din Mareva order and registered caution
key_facts: Mr Kastner invested in Mr Jason's business and obtained Beth Din freezing orders restraining sale of Jason's home pending a fraud arbitration under Jewish law.
With Beth Din permission Kastner registered a Land Registry caution reciting the orders; Jason promised to comply but sold the house to the Shermans.
The purchasers' solicitor negligently missed the caution; Jason fled abroad after a final Beth Din fraud award of about £237,000.
Kastner sought to enforce an equity against the Shermans by proprietary estoppel or constructive trust based on Jason's promise and the caution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from refusal to treat Beth Din freezing order and caution as creating enforceable proprietary rights against innocent purchasers.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; neither Jewish law nor English proprietary estoppel provided a remedy against the Shermans.
enrichment.ratio: An interim freezing order operates in personam and does not create a security interest; a party's promise to comply cannot give proprietary priority over purchasers without a registrable charge, and a registered caution does not bind innocent buyers where no equitable interest validly attached.
legal_issues: Whether Beth Din Mareva orders create proprietary rights under Jewish or English law
Proprietary estoppel and constructive trust after breach of freezing undertaking
Effect of registered caution against purchasers for value
Enforcement of Jewish law arbitration awards in English courts
linked_authorities: Customs and Excise Commissioners v Barclays Bank plc [2004] EWCA Civ 1555
Midland Bank Trust Co Ltd v Green [1981] AC 513
Z Ltd v A-Z [1982] QB 558

notes: Motor insurer avoided policy for non-disclosure of PGA trainee golf professional status; partial success on commuting declaration only.

enrichment.short_title: Whitlam v KGM: motor insurance non-disclosure of trainee golf professional
key_facts: Mr Whitlam, a shop assistant pursuing PGA training to become a professional golfer, insured his car describing his occupation as shop assistant retailing.
His broker omitted employer details that would have identified a golf shop and triggered insurer rejection on the industry database.
After a fatal road accident following return from a PGA residential course he was acquitted of careless driving but the insurer repudiated for innocent material non-disclosure.
The judge declared avoidance valid for failing to disclose trainee professional golfer status but also for commuting to non-permanent workplaces.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on insurer's declaration that motor policy was avoided for material non-disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed only to discharge the declaration relating to use for places of work other than a permanent workplace; main avoidance for occupation non-disclosure upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Innocent non-disclosure of occupation as trainee golf professional, especially with incomplete employer information on a proposal form, is material because it misstates the insured risk; annual PGA courses and amateur tournaments do not necessarily amount to commuting to various workplaces.
legal_issues: Materiality of describing a trainee golf professional as shop assistant
Whether PGA training and tournaments made vehicle use business commuting
Broker's role in completing proposal forms
Insurer entitlement to avoid for innocent non-disclosure

confidence.notes: Full judgment on unusual insurance facts with limited partial allowance of appeal.

notes: Youth Court committal of 14-year-olds for spatula indecent assault quashed; grave crimes procedure wrongly applied.

enrichment.short_title: R (H) v Southampton Youth Court: committal of 14-year-olds for indecent assault
key_facts: Three 14-year-old boys were charged with indecent assault after a BB-gun game ended with one boy restrained and a kitchen spatula inserted between another's buttocks.
The defendants admitted parts of the incident but described it as a stupid joke without sexual motivation; all were of prior good character.
Southampton Youth Court committed them for Crown Court trial on grave crimes grounds anticipating a section 91 custodial sentence approaching two years.
The victim suffered bullying at school and behavioural effects, but the prosecution did not establish sexual gratification as a purpose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of Youth Court decision to commit 14-year-olds for trial rather than retain jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Youth Court decisions quashed for all three claimants and remitted for hearing in the Youth Court; permission granted out of time for A and O.
enrichment.ratio: Committal under section 24 requires a real possibility of a section 91(3) sentence of at least around two years; on these facts a stupid non-sexual assault by first offenders did not justify grave crimes committal and the Youth Court decision was Wednesbury unreasonable.
legal_issues: Whether indecent assault by 14-year-olds warranted grave crimes committal
Meaning of real possibility of a section 91(3) long custodial sentence
Relevance of absence of sexual motivation and prior good character
Procedural fairness where magistrates' reasons were prepared post-decision
linked_authorities: W v Southampton Youth Court [2003] EWHC 1179 (Admin)
R (H) v Southampton Youth Court [2004] EWHC 2912 (Admin)

notes: Interim Protection from Harassment Act injunction for guinea pig farm against animal rights activists; full hearing listed.

enrichment.short_title: Hall v Stop Newchurch Guinea Pigs: interim harassment injunction
key_facts: The Hall family bred guinea pigs for medical research at Darley Oaks Farm, Newchurch, and faced a long campaign of protests and hundreds of incidents since 1999.
Animal rights groups planned an Oxford demonstration in December 2004 amid recent arson against a supplier; the claimants sought urgent interim protection.
Inspector Bird evidenced over 480 incidents since 2003 including criminal damage, intimidation and supplier withdrawal affecting farm operations.
Hodge J made a holding interim injunction with exclusion zones but refused overly wide road restrictions and community-wide protection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court interim application under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 on short notice before planned protest.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted with defined exclusion zones and supplier protection; full four-day hearing listed for 17 January 2005; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: A course of conduct including lawful protest combined with criminal harassment can support interim injunctive relief where a reasonable person would regard the conduct as harassment; interim orders balance protection of research farmers and suppliers against proportionate protest rights pending trial.
legal_issues: Whether Protection from Harassment Act 1997 applies to unincorporated associations
Appropriate scope of exclusion zones around protest targets
Interim test for harassment injunctive relief without final fact findings
Whether residents and community members could be protected persons

notes: Dublin Convention removal certification challenge after Razgar; Beatson J dismissed and made £800 wasted costs order against claimant solicitors.

enrichment.short_title: Mehmeti v SSHD: certification of Dublin Convention removal claim
key_facts: Mrs Mehmeti, a Kosovan dependent on her husband's 1997 asylum claim, faced Dublin Convention removal to Greece after repeated absconding and litigation.
She challenged certification of a 2003 human rights claim as clearly unfounded following the House of Lords decision in Razgar on health-related article 8 removal.
Psychiatric evidence of suicidal ideation if removed was considered but the Secretary of State maintained certification after reconsideration.
The court also addressed late-served medical evidence and made a wasted costs order against the claimant's solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review limited to lawfulness of clearly unfounded certification of a Dublin Convention removal human rights claim.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; certification upheld; wasted costs order of £800 made against claimant solicitors for unreasonable conduct.
enrichment.ratio: After Razgar the court scrutinises certification by asking how an adjudicator would decide, but psychiatric evidence of intermittent suicidal ideation without strong article 8 gravity does not necessarily prevent clearly unfounded certification where immigration control remains a potent proportionality factor.
legal_issues: Application of Razgar five-question approach to certification review
Whether psychiatric evidence of suicidal ideation prevents section 93(2)(b) certification
Article 8(2) proportionality in Dublin Convention return cases
Use of up-to-date medical evidence on certification challenges
